member.name: T:Realm.Ecs.ComponentTypeRegistry
member.summary:
The identifier each component type is known by inside this process. The canonical types are registered up front and take the index of their entry in that list, so their identifiers are fixed and comparable between builds. Any other type is assigned the next identifier the first time it is touched, which means the identifier depends on first-touch order and is therefore only meaningful in this process: canonical identifiers are the ones that cross the wire, through the replicated component table, and a dynamic identifier never does.
The registry is owned by whichever thread touches a type first, and the lock is what makes that first touch single. A canonical identifier is assigned once while the type is loaded, so the lock is not on any steady-state path; a dynamic type is the case to keep out of a publish lane, because assigning one there also creates the component buffer on that lane, and the world refuses a structural change made under a worker lease.

member.name: T:Realm.Ecs.ContentIdStore
member.summary: Owns the single table that every process uses to translate content identifiers into the values they stand for, starting with text and structured to hold further payload kinds in the same identifier space.
member.remarks:
Identifiers are content hashes rather than allocation sequence numbers, so the host, the client and the map script sandbox agree on the identifier for a given payload without sharing any state. Two payloads of the same kind that hash to the same primary identifier are resolved at registration time: the later one receives an identifier from the reserved fallback range so no two values alias. Colliding payloads are reported through and because the fallback decision is only reachable once both payloads have been registered in the same process.
Registration is serialized on the thread that registers, because resolving a collision has to be atomic with the lookup that found it. Reading is not: entries are immutable once stored, so they are published into a concurrent table and a snapshot lane resolves identifiers per unit per codec without ever acquiring the registration lock. The ordered text walk reads a published view of the text table as well, so a peer's cursor copies the entries it is owed without waiting for the registration lock that a lane describing another peer would otherwise hold against it.

member.name: T:Realm.Ecs.ColdPayloadStore`1
member.summary: The payloads a world keeps outside its component arrays, addressed by handle. The simulation thread is the only writer, because handles are allocated, shared and released as entities and components come and go. Readers are not confined to it - a publish lane resolving the payload behind a component handle reads here too - so a write publishes a new immutable view of the table and a read takes one volatile read of it, instead of every reader taking the writer's lock.
